title: Physiology II: Cardiovascular and Respiratory (PIO 214)
description: The cardiac cycle, ECG, cardiac output, blood pressure regulation, pulmonary mechanics, gas exchange and the control of breathing.

topics.title: Cardiac Muscle, the Cardiac Cycle and Heart Sounds
topics.summary: Pacemaker potentials, phases of the cardiac cycle, pressures and heart sounds.

notes.b: SA node cells have an unstable resting potential (pacemaker potential) due to the 'funny' Na+ current (If) and T-type Ca2+ channels; their action potential upstroke is due to Ca2+ influx. The SA node fires at about 60–100/min; the AV node delays conduction (~0.1 s) so the atria empty before ventricular systole. Ventricular muscle action potentials have a plateau (phase 2) due to L-type Ca2+ influx, giving a long refractory period that prevents tetanus. Sympathetic stimulation (β1) increases rate and force; vagal (muscarinic M2) stimulation slows the heart.
k: Plateau from L-type Ca2+ → long refractory period

notes.b: At a heart rate of 75/min the cycle lasts 0.8 s (systole ≈ 0.3 s, diastole ≈ 0.5 s). Phases: atrial systole; isovolumetric ventricular contraction (all valves closed); ventricular ejection; isovolumetric relaxation; rapid and slow ventricular filling. The first heart sound (S1) is closure of the AV (mitral and tricuspid) valves at the start of systole; the second (S2) is closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves at the start of diastole. A third sound (S3) occurs with rapid ventricular filling; a fourth (S4) with atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle. Diastole shortens most as heart rate rises, reducing coronary perfusion time.
k: S1: AV valves close; S2: semilunar valves close

topics.title: Electrocardiogram and Cardiac Output
topics.summary: ECG waves and intervals, cardiac output, stroke volume and the Frank–Starling law.

notes.b: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation; the QRS complex ventricular depolarisation (atrial repolarisation is hidden in it); the T wave ventricular repolarisation. Normal PR interval is 0.12–0.20 s (prolonged in first-degree heart block); QRS duration < 0.12 s; the QT interval varies with heart rate. On standard paper (25 mm/s), one small square is 0.04 s and one large square 0.2 s; heart rate ≈ 300 ÷ number of large squares between R waves. Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalaemia.
k: P = atrial depolarisation; QRS = ventricular depolarisation; T = ventricular repolarisation

notes.b: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate (≈ 70 mL × 70/min ≈ 5 L/min at rest). Cardiac index = CO / body surface area. Stroke volume depends on preload (end-diastolic volume), afterload (arterial pressure) and contractility. The Frank–Starling law states that the force of contraction increases with the initial length of cardiac fibres (greater venous return → greater stroke volume), matching the output of the two ventricles. Ejection fraction = SV/EDV, normally about 55–70%.

topics.title: Blood Pressure and Circulation
topics.summary: Haemodynamics, regulation of arterial blood pressure and capillary exchange.

notes.b: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance, and approximately diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure. By Poiseuille's law, resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius, so arterioles (resistance vessels) control flow. Veins hold about 60–70% of blood volume (capacitance vessels). Starling forces govern capillary exchange: hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, plasma oncotic pressure (albumin) pulls it in; oedema results from raised hydrostatic pressure (heart failure), low albumin (nephrotic syndrome, kwashiorkor), increased permeability (inflammation) or lymphatic obstruction (filariasis).
k: MAP = CO × TPR ≈ DBP + ⅓ pulse pressure

notes.b: Short-term control is by the baroreceptor reflex: stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic arch (vagus) signal to the medullary vasomotor centre; a fall in pressure increases sympathetic and reduces vagal activity, raising heart rate, contractility and vasoconstriction. Long-term control is renal: the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (renin from juxtaglomerular cells → angiotensin I → angiotensin II by ACE in the lungs → vasoconstriction and aldosterone release → Na+ and water retention), antidiuretic hormone, and atrial natriuretic peptide (which promotes Na+ excretion).
k: Baroreceptors: carotid sinus (IX) and aortic arch (X)
RAAS: renin → Ang I → (ACE) → Ang II → aldosterone

topics.title: Mechanics of Breathing and Lung Volumes
topics.summary: Inspiration and expiration, compliance, surfactant, lung volumes and capacities.

notes.b: Quiet inspiration is active: the diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3–C5) contracts and external intercostals raise the ribs, lowering intrapleural pressure (normally about −5 cmH2O) and drawing air in. Quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil. Compliance is the change in volume per unit change in pressure; it falls in pulmonary fibrosis and rises in emphysema. Surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine), secreted by type II pneumocytes from about 24–28 weeks' gestation, lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse; deficiency in premature babies causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (prevented by antenatal corticosteroids).
k: Diaphragm: phrenic nerve C3–C5 ('C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive')

notes.b: Typical adult values: tidal volume (TV) 500 mL; inspiratory reserve volume ≈ 3,000 mL; expiratory reserve volume ≈ 1,100 mL; residual volume (RV) ≈ 1,200 mL (cannot be measured by simple spirometry). Capacities: vital capacity = IRV + TV + ERV (≈ 4,600 mL); functional residual capacity = ERV + RV (≈ 2,300 mL); total lung capacity ≈ 5,800 mL. Anatomical dead space is about 150 mL; alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space) × respiratory rate. FEV1/FVC is reduced (< 0.7) in obstructive disease (asthma, COPD) and normal or increased in restrictive disease.
k: RV cannot be measured by spirometry

topics.title: Gas Exchange, Oxygen Transport and Control of Breathing
topics.summary: Partial pressures, the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve, CO2 transport and respiratory control.

notes.b: Normal arterial PO2 is about 100 mmHg (13.3 kPa) and PCO2 40 mmHg (5.3 kPa). About 98% of oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin; each gram of Hb carries about 1.34 mL O2. The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid; P50 is about 27 mmHg. The curve shifts right (reduced affinity, more unloading) with increased CO2, H+ (the Bohr effect), temperature and 2,3-BPG; HbF and carbon monoxide shift it left. CO2 is carried mainly as bicarbonate (~70%, formed by carbonic anhydrase in red cells, with the chloride shift), as carbamino compounds (~23%) and dissolved (~7%).

Respiratory rhythm is generated in the medulla (pre-Bötzinger complex; dorsal and ventral respiratory groups) and modified by pontine centres. Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to H+ in cerebrospinal fluid, reflecting arterial PCO2 — the main drive to breathe. Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond mainly to low PO2 (below about 60 mmHg), and also to raised PCO2 and H+. In chronic CO2 retention (e.g. severe COPD) hypoxic drive may become more important. At high altitude, hypoxia stimulates ventilation and, over time, erythropoietin release.
k: CO2 (via central chemoreceptors) is the main respiratory drive
Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to PO2 < 60 mmHg
